fields.headline: Corrections and clarifications
fields.bodyText: • A review of the documentary Steal This Story, Please! (14 August, G2, p8) incorrectly said that the journalist Amy Goodman had worked on the Phil Donahue Show. In fact, she had speculatively contacted the TV show to get a job there as a producer. • A live music review described Luke Combs as the “highest-selling country artist of all time”, but according to the Recording Industry Association of America he was overtaken in December by Morgan Wallen (Arena-sized swagger from a regular Joe megastar, 27 July, p17). Other recently amended articles include: Destroyed crops, riverbed cyclists and a ‘Rock of Starvation’: how drought has devastated the Danube ‘They’re anxious about everything’: life for young people seeking work in Dudley and Lewisham Iga Swiatek takes swing at critics after ending title drought in Canada It’s the SUV tyranny: where have all the normal family cars gone? Novak Djokovic suffers in Cincinnati heat as Thiago Agustín Tirante inflicts shock defeat Why cancer, not cost of living, may be the biggest issue in Iowa’s midterm elections ‘The spirit of resistance’: De Gaulle biopic turns into surprise hit for France’s younger viewers North Sydney pool closed a week after much-hyped reopening following $122m overhaul Joy in Hollywood as historic Cinerama dome to reopen: ‘People still want to go to the movies’ New York City man charged with hate crimes after alleged synagogue assault Editorial complaints and correction requests can be sent to: guardian.readers@theguardian.com. You can also write to: Readers’ editor, Kings Place, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU, or leave a voicemail on +44 (0) 20 3353 4736.

webTitle: Trump cuts US-South Korea military drills citing ‘good relationship with Kim Jong-un’ | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: Trump cuts US-South Korea military drills citing ‘good relationship with Kim Jong-un’
fields.trailText: President said he was ‘not happy’ with plans for large-scale joint exercises he described as ‘inappropriate and hostile’
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Donald Trump has said he is scaling back joint US military drills with South Korea aimed at deterring North Korea, despite military officials from both countries warning that Kim Jong-un’s regime is learning new battlefield tactics from the Ukraine war. The president said he was “not happy” with US participation “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong-un”. He added that the drills were costly and “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a country that, as long as Donald J Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful”. Trump added that it was too late to cancel the drills so he had ordered the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to “substantially reduce” them. Why are there continuing concerns about USS Abraham Lincoln? Democrats have intensified their demands for answers from the Trump administration over conditions onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln amid concern over crew morale, mental health and living conditions. Ruben Gallego, a Democratic senator from Arizona, said he blamed the carrier’s prolonged deployment on the unresolved war that Donald Trump started in February with Iran as well as lackluster leadership in general from the Republican president’s administration. Jared Kushner meets Hamas leader before talks with Netanyahu on Gaza Donald Trump’s son-in-law and envoy, Jared Kushner, held a rare meeting with Hamas’s political chief on Sunday in Egypt, in a new diplomatic effort to make progress on the stalled Gaza ceasefire. On Monday, Kushner will meet Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, who is under pressure after rejecting the new 15-point, US-backed roadmap. The roadmap involves Hamas gradually giving up its weapons while Israeli forces halt attacks and begin withdrawing from Gaza. Netanyahu says Israel will not retreat from any position in Gaza until Hamas has been completely disarmed. Israel has killed more than 1,200 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded more than 4,100 since agreeing to the ceasefire on 10 October 2025, according to Gaza’s health ministry. Todd Blanche declines to pledge independence from White House The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, on Sunday declined to assure that the federal justice department he helms would always act independently of the White House and Donald Trump. “No attorney general should ever pledge that,” he said on NBC. Blanche also claimed Trump would never ask him to do something that crossed an ethical or legal line. Blanche added: “I swore to the constitution of the United States, like every cabinet secretary has done, and like every attorney general before me has done. And so this narrative that’s mostly pushed by the left and pushed by the media that the president’s going to pull me aside and ask me to do something illegal is completely a false narrative, not true, will not happen and hasn’t happened.” Republican senator denounces Trump’s ‘crazy, stupid’ claims about MMR vaccine safety The Republican senator Bill Cassidy, a medical doctor who voted to confirm the anti-vaccine activist Robert F Kennedy as federal health secretary in early 2025, on Sunday denounced Donald Trump’s “crazy, stupid” claims about the safety of the combined MMR vaccine for undermining faith in immunization. Asked about Trump’s comment that “nothing bad can happen” from advising parents to get six separate shots for their children instead of two, Cassidy told CNN on Sunday: “If it wasn’t so potentially tragic, you would break out laughing at a comment like that.” In other news … Hayden Panettiere, the actor known for her roles in television shows such as Heroes and Nashville, has died at the age of 36. Her father, Skip Panettiere, asked for privacy “as our family takes time to process this unimaginable loss”. Kyiv could hit Russia with its own domestic ballistic missiles in months, a former defense minister has said. Wildlife groups in Florida are celebrating record numbers of sea turtle nests this season, but experts warn Donald Trump’s recent gutting of the Endangered Species Act could reverse decades of their recovery. Tommy John, synonymous with a ligament-replacement surgery that paved a path to recovery for injured baseball players, has died. He was 83. The left-hander was 31 years old when he tore the ulnar collateral ligament in his pitching elbow and had it replaced with a tendon from his right forearm. The University of Cambridge has defended its mental health support for the academic Jason Arday. Arday was pronounced dead on Friday, weeks after he resigned from his post as professor of sociology of education, following widespread press coverage of accusations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements. Stat of the day: At least six people dead from days of storms and record flooding in Indiana A four-year-old boy, two men and three women were among those who died since storms began on 11 August in Indiana, the state’s homeland security department spokesperson, Liz Woods, said. Building power: Teenagers demand more support after US schools ban phones More students are advocating for their own digital wellbeing and developing programs to thrive in tech-free learning environments. Don’t miss this: Why cancer, not cost of living, may be the biggest issue in Iowa’s midterm elections The midwestern state of Iowa has the second highest rate of cancer nationwide and is one of only three states where incidents of the disease are rising. Promises to address the issue are now top of mind for candidates ahead of the 3 November elections, in which Iowa may play an important role in deciding control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s term. … or this: The Fair Hill Five, horse racing’s bizarre transatlantic betting coup, explained Someone, somewhere, appears to have made a lot of money by betting on a series of unfancied horses who all unexpectedly came good. Bryan Armen Graham looks at what could be a sensational stroke of luck … or something more sinister. Climate check: Spotlight on UN desertification summit as it mulls how to spend $12bn war chest Environment editor Fiona Harvey reports that as swathes of the northern hemisphere bake in what could be the hottest year on record, with wildfires blazing across North America and Europe and heatwaves afflicting millions across Asia, the UN’s biannual talks on desertification have assumed much greater importance – and have started attracting more money. Last Thing: Europe’s tallest Virgin Mary statue unveiled in small Polish village A small village in Poland with a population of just 150 has put itself on the map by unveiling what is believed to be – at 182ft – Europe’s tallest statue of the Virgin Mary. webTitle: A tale of two Dan Sullivans: Republicans with same name contest Alaska primary

fields.headline: A tale of two Dan Sullivans: Republicans with same name contest Alaska primary
fields.trailText: Democrat Mary Peltola, who won the red state’s House seat twice, is also running to unseat the incumbent senator
fields.bodyText: Dan J Sullivan is a retired schoolteacher and US Forest Service employee living in the town of Petersburg in south-eastern Alaska, who is running as a Republican for the US Senate. Dan S Sullivan is a Republican US senator, who has represented Alaska since 2015. Both candidates will appear on the ballot, one name after the other, when Alaskans vote in primary elections this week – a complicated quirk of the contest that has drawn howls from Republicans. But the incumbent senator’s real threat, Alaska politics watchers say, is Mary Peltola, a Democrat who managed to twice win election to the state’s seat in the US House of Representatives, and is now vying tobeat him in November’s midterm elections in the US Senate. The Tuesday vote in the non-partisan primary will see four candidates advance to the general election for the seat in November. Though no Democrat has been elected to the US Senate from Alaska since 2008, the party believes Peltola is the right candidate to flip the seat, and her victory would put Democrats well on their way to retaking control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. “The reason Mary Peltola has a chance is not because, necessarily, Democrats are surging in Alaska,” said Scott Kendall, an election law attorney who has worked for candidates of both parties, including the senator Sullivan. “It’s that Mary Peltola, you know, she’s very pro-oil and gas development. She’s good on issues that matter to Alaskans’ pocketbooks, and that makes her just a bit of a unicorn.” The largest state in the union but physically separated from the lower 48, Alaska has unique politics. With an economy heavily reliant on oil and gas production, the state’s Democrats tend to advocate for expanded production, in contrast with their counterparts elsewhere, who are concerned about fossil fuels’ role in driving the climate crisis. While Alaska has only once voted for a Democrat in a presidential election – Lyndon B Johnson, in 1964 – power has oscillated between the two parties at the state level, and bipartisan coalitions today control both the state house and senate. Independents make up two-thirds of registered voters and Republicans about 23%, while fewer than 12% of Alaskans are Democrats. Sullivan won election in 2014 after beating the first-term Democratic senator Mark Begich, and has been a reliable Republican vote in his two terms, hewing much closer to his party’s agenda than the state’s senior Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski, who has grown prominent nationwide for repeatedly bucking Trump. Peltola cracked the GOP’s dominance of the state’s federal delegation in 2022 when Don Young, the Republican who had represented the state’s at-large US House district since 1973, died suddenly. She triumphed in the special election to finish his term, becoming the first Alaska Native ever to serve in Congress, and won a full term later that year. In 2024, Republican Nick Begich III narrowly defeated her bid for re-election. Alaska voted for Trump by more than 13 percentage points that year, but Peltola is viewed as Democrats’ best bet for the Senate race in one of a handful of red states the party is targeting to win back a majority in the upper chamber. Seeking to prove that she can better advocate for the state’s specific interests and needs in Washington, Peltola has put her moderate brand of politics at the center of her campaign. Her slogan “fish, family, freedom” is a nod both to the cultural importance of fishing in Alaska – and especially to its native communities, which form a potent political bloc – and to the issue of bycatch, whereby trawlers pick up valuable catches like crab and salmon in their nets, harming sport and commercial fishers alike. “Fish has always been, really, a passion issue in Alaska,” said Joelle Hall, president of the Alaska AFL-CIO, which has endorsed Peltola. Hall credited the former congresswoman with making the issue of bycatch and the health of the fishing industry in general more prominent in the state’s politics. During her time in the House of Representatives, Peltola advocated for Joe Biden to approve Willow, one of the biggest oil and gas developments in decades. The decision raised the hackles of environmentalists for its potential to drive global heating, but Hall describes it as huge for unionized workers. “We are also in the middle of a little bit of an oil and gas boom in Alaska,” said Hall. “That’s because Mary Peltola brought us the Willow project with the Biden administration.” Peltola may be further boosted by national trends breaking in Democrats’ favor. Trump’s approval ratings are low in the state as they are nationwide, while gas prices in Alaska have shot up since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, and are now among the highest nationwide. Polls have recently found the two candidates neck-and-neck before the November election, and major election forecasters view Sullivan’s re-election bid as a toss-up. A former marine who served as the state’s attorney general and natural resources commissioner, Dan S Sullivan has emphasized his focus on military affairs in a state with a large number of bases and veterans, as well as his own efforts to preserve the state’s fisheries. Steve Frank, a Republican former state senator, said that despite Peltola’s efforts to see Willow approved, he believed Sullivan would be a more reliable advocate for the state’s economically vital oil industry, especially with the presidential administration set to change in another two years. “The federal government views us kind of like a colony, and they forget that we’re American citizens trying to earn a living up here,” said Frank, referencing moves by the Biden administration to protect tracts of Alaska land and water from oil drilling. “And so they tend to want to lock us up, keep us from developing our resources, and so he’s pushing back against that.” The race has seen major spending, with the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund announcing it will put $17m towards helping Sullivan, while the Democrats’ Senate Majority Pac invested $12m into backing Peltola. Federal Election Commission filings until the end of July show Peltola has outraised Sullivan, bringing in $18.5m to his $11.7m, with $4.6m on hand compared with the Republican’s $7.3m. Meanwhile, OpenSecrets, a non-profit that tracks campaign donations, reported that two Super Pacs (political action committees) have spent a combined nearly $2m in Alaska recently to back other candidates who could syphon votes from both Peltola and Sullivan. Also on the ballot in Tuesday’s election will be Nick Begich III, who is vying for a second term against independent Bill Hill, the main challenger for the House seat after Democrat Matt Schultz dropped out and endorsed him. Alaskans will also select candidates to replace governor Mike Dunleavy, the Republican incumbent who is barred by term limits from seeking re-election. Dan J Sullivan of Petersburg, Alaska, who did not respond to a request for comment, is listed just above the senator among the 16 names running for Senate, though Dan S Sullivan has “registered Republican” and “incumbent” next to his name. The GOP went to court to boot Dan J Sullivan from the race, arguing that he was a “sham” contender propped up by Democrats to confuse voters and undermine Senator Sullivan, but were unsuccessful. Though it’s a marquee race of this year’s US Senate elections, when it comes to Alaska-specific issues, Kendall predicted there may wind up being less daylight than would be expected between Peltola and Sullivan on Alaska-specific issues. “I think she would probably frustrate a lot of Democrats, if I’m being honest. I think she would be, to national Democrats, what Lisa Murkowski is to national Republicans,” said Kendall. “There’ll be a moment where a Democratic president says something like: ‘Well, I want to turn this huge swath of Alaska into a wilderness preserve, no hunting, no fishing, no development,’” he suggested. “She’s going to balk at that.”

webTitle: Trump’s tough-guy image has been undone by his own actions | Mohamad Bazzi

fields.headline: Trump’s tough-guy image has been undone by his own actions
fields.trailText: The president was forced to hide in a catering truck amid the Iran war, in an encapsulation of the conflict’s failures
fields.bodyText: For decades, Donald Trump cultivated a public image based on strength and dominance. He was a brash New York real estate mogul; a reality TV star who deployed his signature phrase: “You’re fired!” to eliminate contestants from The Apprentice; and eventually US president and undisputed leader of the Republican party. In recent months, Trump has taken his boastfulness to an extreme, reportedly telling confidants that he’s “the most powerful person to ever live” and comparing himself with some of history’s most feared leaders, including Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Hitler, Stalin and Mao. But recent revelations have threatened to shatter Trump’s image as a strongman: the US president departed on a secret military flight out of Turkey after attending a Nato summit, while the White House told the public he was flying onboard Air Force One. The operation involved an elaborate ruse in which Trump boarded his jumbo jet in view of TV cameras, and then was hustled out by the Secret Service through an airport catering truck. Trump was taken to an alternate military aircraft, which flew him to Britain – all unbeknown to journalists and several White House staff members who stayed on Air Force One and thought they were on the same plane as the president. The embarrassing necessity was a result of Trump’s unnecessary war against Iran. US officials used such levels of subterfuge because they were worried about an Iranian assassination attempt against Trump, according to reports in the Washington Post and New York Times. On 11 August, Trump confirmed that he had secretly switched planes in Turkey, and attributed the decision to his protective detail and military advisers. “I go by Secret Service and the military,” Trump told reporters who asked why US officials had used such an intricate ploy and kept the public in the dark about it until the story was leaked. “They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane. Equal safety. But they wanted me to do it, so I do it. I do what they say.” Trump tried to evade criticism that the decision left several cabinet members and senior White House officials – including Marco Rubio, the secretary of state; Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary; Stephen Miller, Trump’s top domestic adviser; and Steven Cheung, the White House communications director – on Air Force One to serve as decoys, along with other Trump staffers and journalists. To deflect more questions, Trump claimed, without providing evidence, that the secret military plane he flew on was actually at “greater risk” than the Air Force One jet that the world saw him board after the Nato summit. “I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for,” he said. It’s easy to see why Trump and his administration did not want to publicly share details of the ruse after the danger had passed, as past presidents had done when they used subterfuge to visit war zones and other hazardous locations. The image of Trump hiding in an airport catering container to avoid a potential Iranian assassination attempt is a stark contrast to the tough guy brand he spent years cultivating. It’s also an antithesis to the image Trump projected after he survived an assassination attempt at a presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. In a series of photos captured by news photographers at the scene, Trump raised his fist in the air and mouthed the words: “Fight, fight, fight” to supporters as he was rushed off stage by Secret Service agents, bleeding from his ear. One image in particular, showing a bloodied Trump pumping his fist with a US flag in the background, became iconic – and his campaign quickly tried to monetize it by using the photo on the cover of a book and to sell $299 Trump-branded sneakers. Beyond the dueling imagery, the fact that Trump took refuge in a catering truck has deeper political implications. It encapsulates Trump’s failure in his war on Iran: a president who constantly boasts about US military prowess and tries to project personal strength instead appears weak in front of the world as he hides from the consequences of his own actions. Nearly six months ago, Trump launched his reckless war against Iran as an act of imperial hubris – and a culmination of a series of lawless acts since he returned to office in 2025. With little resistance from the Republican-controlled Congress or the US supreme court, Trump was able to gut government agencies, use federal law enforcement to target his political enemies, appoint his loyalists as top prosecutors, deploy national guard troops into US cities, and weaken decades-old anti-corruption laws designed to constrain presidential power after the Watergate scandal. He also steamrolled over Congress and its authority to declare war. In late February, when the US and Israel launched a series of devastating airstrikes against Iran, Trump had expansive goals: to destroy Tehran’s military capabilities and nuclear program, and to topple Iran’s theocratic regime by decimating its leadership and instigating a popular uprising. In the war’s early days, the US and Israel assassinated more than 30 senior Iranian military and political officials, including the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. But the Iranian system proved resilient and it quickly replaced those officials, partly by appointing Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba, as the new supreme leader, to ensure continuity. Iran also turned its proximity to the strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which more than a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed each day, into an effective economic weapon. Tehran closed the passageway at the start of the war, increasing energy prices and disrupting the global economy. Since then, Trump has struggled to reach a deal with Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz and prevent the war from spiraling into a regional conflict that could cause severe economic damage. For months, Trump has tried to negotiate a face-saving agreement that would allow him to declare victory and shift US public attention away from the war before midterm elections in November that could see Republicans lose control of Congress. Iran’s leaders and Trump both say they don’t trust the other side to abide by any agreement – and a memorandum of understanding reached in mid-June, which included reopening the strait of Hormuz and lifting a US naval blockade against Iranian ships in the region, has collapsed. Since then, tit-for-tat attacks by Iran and the US have rekindled fears of another all-out war. Not surprisingly, Iranian officials and state media are reveling in the extensive media attention over Trump secretly switching planes in Turkey – and especially the detail about him being ushered into an airport catering truck. A presenter on Iranian state TV called it a “scandal stemming from fear of Iran’s military power”, and described the incident as a source of “humiliation” for the US president. It will take time for Trump to undo the damage this ruse has done to his self-proclaimed image as a strong and dominant world leader. More importantly, his disastrous decision to launch a war against Iran will shape his legacy long after he leaves office. Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University

webTitle: Who is Hasan Piker – and why are some Australian conservatives outraged about his return to the ABC?

fields.headline: Who is Hasan Piker – and why are some Australian conservatives outraged about his return to the ABC?
fields.trailText: The leftwing commentator has been invited to appear on the Planet America program on Monday night
fields.bodyText: The ABC is set to air the return of its Planet America program on Monday night as the US midterm elections gain steam, with a new episode featuring the leftwing commentator Hasan Piker. Host John Barron said the episode will focus on the “rise of Democratic socialists and the populist left”, with Piker speaking about “what it’s like in the eye of a political storm”. But the appearance quickly sparked the ire of conservatives in Australia. News Corp’s News24 host James Morrow was deeply critical of the interview on Friday, wondering if there was “something in the water at the ABC’s Ultimo HQ that makes them think they are immune to consequences”. “If the ABC wants to have this clown on their network, that’s their business, but let them do it without our tax dollars,” he challenged last week. Barron has urged critics to watch the appearance before casting judgment, saying he’s not surprised that “some of the usual suspects are outraged, OUTRAGED, that we would even speak to Piker”. “Like it or not, he’s a central figure in the 2026 US election,” Barron wrote on X. “I was prepared to talk to Piker about his role in this election just as I was prepared to talk to @seanhannity about his role in the 2012 election … relevance.” So who is Hasan Piker, and why does he have some in a tailspin? Streaming to millions Piker, 35, is an extremely popular figure in left-leaning politics in the US, with more than 3 million followers on Twitch and millions more on YouTube and Instagram. He streams on the internet nearly every day, sometimes for eight hours at a time, and has been heralded as a modern-day kingmaker for progressive Democrats. He has built a legion of fans – many whom are young men – with regular discourse about American foreign policy, capitalism, his support for LGBTQ+ rights and for a willingness to heap criticism on the Democratic establishment. He’s described himself as a “megaphone”, amplifying frustrations with “establishment liberalism”, not as a change maker himself. His readiness to champion progressive challengers over established figures has angered some top Democrats. He’s also become a frequent target of the Murdoch empire in the US, with Fox News publishing running criticism of his commentary. Piker’s opinions are unfiltered and, at times, extreme. In 2019, as part of a broader critique of American foreign policy, he said the US “deserved” the September 11 terrorist attacks (he later apologised for the remark). He’s also a frequent and vocal critic of Israel’s leadership and claimed he would “vote for Hamas over Israel every single time”. He maintains he’s not antisemitic, but strongly against Zionism and the country’s policy on the war in Gaza and Palestinians. “I have no issues getting vilified by people on the right. I love when my enemies hate me,” he told the Guardian in December. “It is what it is: they talk shit; what are you gonna do?” But Piker’s comments have landed him in hot water. The British government banned him from entering the country for a speaking engagement in June, saying at the time his presence “may not be conducive to the public good”. Complaints to ABC Piker was last on the ABC in September to speak about the assassination of the conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The streamer spoke to Sarah Ferguson for 7.30, saying he was “horrified” at the killing, which came just weeks before the pair were set to debate each other. The appearance prompted 68 complaints to the ABC, with viewers suggesting the national broadcaster should not have platformed Piker “as he is a far-left extremist” and had made “unsupported adverse claims about Mr Kirk’s past remarks”. The ombudsman determined the appearance did not breach the ABC’s editorial standards. Ferguson also interviewed Trump kingmaker Steve Bannon during the US president’s first administration, which prompted its own criticism. The ABC did not have an ombudsman at the time. Morrow wondered if Piker’s latest appearance could lead to a similar outcome, pointing to the ABC bowing to criticism in recent weeks. The network’s managing director, Hugh Marks, apologised to Gina Rinehart after airing a short documentary for its Race Around the World program that included crude and offensive comments about the mining billionaire. While the ABC ombudsman found it did not breach any editorial policies, Marks said it had fallen “short of community expectations” and that the ABC would change its editorial guidance. ‘It makes sense to hear from him’ Barron has defended the interview on X in recent days, saying Piker’s position in American politics is more relevant than ever due to the surge in progressive Democrats. “He’s become a central figure in this year’s election, it makes sense to hear from him,” Barron wrote to a critic about Piker. Barron said he had also interviewed Roger Stone, a longtime friend and ally of Trump who was sentenced to three years in prison in 2020 before he was granted clemency by the president. “If you watch, I’ll be interested to know if it confirms your concerns or overcomes them,” he went on. “Either way, we choose guests of all stripes based on interest and relevance.”
